DEFERRED SALE OF HOME ORDER ("DUKE ORDER") — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Deferred Sale of Home Order Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, whose proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties is pending, has concluded by judgment, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes what California law says about a "deferred sale of home order" — the order, sometimes called a "Duke order" after the decision that first approved the practice, by which a California family court temporarily delays the sale of the family home and awards its temporary exclusive use and possession to a custodial parent. It states, in general terms, the statutory definitions in Family Code section 3800, the threshold economic-feasibility determination required by section 3801, the discretionary factors listed in section 3802, what the order must and may contain under sections 3803, 3804, and 3806, the reservation of jurisdiction required by section 3809, the modification and termination provisions of sections 3807 and 3808, the chapter's applicability rule in section 3810, and how two published California decisions have described the doctrine's judicial origin and its statutory scope. This information sheet does not determine, calculate, or assert that a deferred sale of home order would or would not be economically feasible in the circumstances of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, that any such order is or is not necessary to minimize the adverse impact of the proceeding on any child, how any listed factor weighs on these facts, or whether any change in circumstances has occurred; those are matters for the court to decide on the specific evidence before it, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to address by their own written agreement.

WHAT A DEFERRED SALE OF HOME ORDER IS — FAMILY CODE SECTION 3800 DEFINITIONS
Family Code section 3800 supplies the three defined terms used throughout the chapter on deferred sale of home orders (Family Code sections 3800 through 3810). Subdivision (a) defines "custodial parent" as a party awarded physical custody of a child. Subdivision (b) defines a "deferred sale of home order" as an order that temporarily delays the sale of the family home and awards its temporary exclusive use and possession to a custodial parent of a minor child, or of a child for whom support is authorized under Family Code sections 3900 and 3901 (support of a minor child and of an unmarried full-time high school student under 19) or under section 3910 (support of an adult child incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means), whether or not the custodial parent has sole or joint custody, in order to minimize the adverse impact of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties on the welfare of the child. Subdivision (c) defines "resident parent" as a party who has requested, or who has already been awarded, a deferred sale of home order. By the terms of subdivision (b), the order is an order about the timing of a sale and about temporary use and possession; the definition does not describe it as an award of ownership of the home to either party.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3800(a) (California Legislative Information text), definition of "custodial parent" for the deferred sale of home order chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3800.)
  "“Deferred sale of home order” means an order that temporarily delays the sale and awards the temporary exclusive use and possession of the family home to a custodial parent of a minor child or child for whom support is authorized under Sections 3900 and 3901 or under Section 3910, whether or not the custodial parent has sole or joint custody, in order to minimize the adverse impact of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties on the welfare of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3800(b) (California Legislative Information text), definition of "deferred sale of home order" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3800.)
  "“Resident parent” means a party who has requested or who has already been awarded a deferred sale of home order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3800(c) (California Legislative Information text), definition of "resident parent" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3800.)

Section 3800's definition of "deferred sale of home order" cross-references Family Code sections 3900, 3901, and 3910 for the class of children whose support triggers the chapter; the text and scope of those three support statutes are set by their own provisions and are not quoted or analyzed in this clause, and section 3910 in particular is the subject of a separate information sheet elsewhere in this corpus, which this clause does not restate. Section 3800 does not itself define the term "family home," a gap that a published California decision has expressly noted and that is addressed in this document's separate clause on the judicial construction of the chapter's scope. Nothing in section 3800 states when such an order may be made, who bears any burden, or how long a deferral may last; those points are governed by other sections of the same chapter and are addressed in this document's separate clauses. This clause does not address whether any particular home, occupancy arrangement, or custody arrangement satisfies any part of these definitions.

THE THRESHOLD ECONOMIC-FEASIBILITY DETERMINATION — FAMILY CODE SECTION 3801
Family Code section 3801 sets a threshold the court addresses before it reaches the discretionary question. Subdivision (a) provides that if one of the parties has requested a deferred sale of home order, the court shall first determine whether it is economically feasible to maintain the payments on any note secured by a deed of trust, the property taxes, and the insurance for the home during the period the sale is deferred, and to maintain the condition of the home comparable to its condition at the time of trial. Subdivision (b) directs the court, in making that determination, to consider all of three listed items: the resident parent's income; the availability of spousal support, child support, or both; and any other sources of funds available to make those payments. Subdivision (c) states the Legislature's declared intent in requiring the determination — to avoid the likelihood of possible defaults on note payments and resulting foreclosures, to avoid inadequate insurance coverage, to prevent deterioration of the condition of the family home, and to prevent any other circumstance that would jeopardize both parents' equity in the home.

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3801(c) (California Legislative Information text), the Legislature's declared intent in requiring the determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3801.)

Section 3801 uses the word "first," placing this determination ahead of the section 3802 discretionary decision, but the statute does not state a burden of proof, a standard of proof, or what evidence is required to establish or negate economic feasibility, and this clause does not supply any of those. The section also does not say what happens to a request if the court determines that deferral is not economically feasible. Whether any particular income, support award, or other fund makes a particular deferral economically feasible is a factual question for the court on the evidence, and this clause does not address it.

THE DISCRETIONARY DECISION AND ITS TEN LISTED FACTORS — FAMILY CODE SECTION 3802
Family Code section 3802 governs the decision itself. Subdivision (a) provides that if the court has determined under section 3801 that it is economically feasible to consider ordering a deferred sale of the family home, the court may grant a deferred sale of home order to a custodial parent if the court determines that the order is necessary in order to minimize the adverse impact of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties on the child. The verb is permissive — the court "may" grant the order — and the necessity finding is a precondition to granting it. Subdivision (b) provides that in exercising its discretion to grant or deny the order the court shall consider all of ten listed factors: the length of time the child has resided in the home; the child's placement or grade in school; the accessibility and convenience of the home to the child's school and other services or facilities used by and available to the child, including child care; whether the home has been adapted or modified to accommodate any physical disabilities of a child or a resident parent in a manner that a change in residence may adversely affect the resident parent's ability to meet the child's needs; the emotional detriment to the child associated with a change in residence; the extent to which the location of the home permits the resident parent to continue employment; the financial ability of each parent to obtain suitable housing; the tax consequences to the parents; the economic detriment to the nonresident parent in the event of a deferred sale of home order; and any other factors the court deems just and equitable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "If the court determines pursuant to Section 3801 that it is economically feasible to consider ordering a deferred sale of the family home, the court may grant a deferred sale of home order to a custodial parent if the court determines that the order is necessary in order to minimize the adverse impact of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties on the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3802(a) (California Legislative Information text), the permissive grant and the necessity determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3802.)
  "In exercising its discretion to grant or deny a deferred sale of home order, the court shall consider all of the following:(1) The length of time the child has resided in the home.(2) The child’s placement or grade in school.(3) The accessibility and convenience of the home to the child’s school and other services or facilities used by and available to the child, including child care.(4) Whether the home has been adapted or modified to accommodate any physical disabilities of a child or a resident parent in a manner that a change in residence may adversely affect the ability of the resident parent to meet the needs of the child.(5) The emotional detriment to the child associated with a change in residence.(6) The extent to which the location of the home permits the resident parent to continue employment.(7) The financial ability of each parent to obtain suitable housing.(8) The tax consequences to the parents.(9) The economic detriment to the nonresident parent in the event of a deferred sale of home order.(10) Any other factors the court deems just and equitable."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3802(b) (California Legislative Information text), the ten factors the court shall consider in exercising its discretion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3802.)

WHAT THE ORDER STATES, RECORDING IT, AND MAINTENANCE AND IMPROVEMENT COSTS — FAMILY CODE SECTIONS 3803, 3804, AND 3806
Three sections of the chapter address the content and mechanics of the order. Family Code section 3803 provides that a deferred sale of home order shall state the duration of the order and may include the legal description and the assessor's parcel number of the real property subject to the order — the duration is mandatory content, the property identifiers are optional content. Family Code section 3804 provides that a deferred sale of home order may be recorded in the office of the county recorder of the county in which the real property is located; recording is permissive under the statute's own terms, not required. Family Code section 3806 provides that the court may make an order specifying the parties' respective responsibilities for the payment of the costs of routine maintenance and of capital improvements.

MANDATORY RESERVATION OF JURISDICTION OVER ISSUES ARISING FROM THE ORDER — FAMILY CODE SECTION 3809
Family Code section 3809 provides that in making an order under the deferred sale of home order chapter, the court shall reserve jurisdiction to determine any issues that arise with respect to the deferred sale of home order, including but not limited to the maintenance of the home and the tax consequences to each party. The reservation is stated in mandatory terms — the court "shall" reserve jurisdiction — and the two named subjects, maintenance and tax consequences, are expressly illustrative rather than exhaustive.

  "In making an order pursuant to this chapter, the court shall reserve jurisdiction to determine any issues that arise with respect to the deferred sale of home order including, but not limited to, the maintenance of the home and the tax consequences to each party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3809 (California Legislative Information text), mandatory reservation of jurisdiction over issues arising from the order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3809.)

Section 3809 states that jurisdiction is reserved but does not state for how long, what procedure a party uses to bring a reserved issue before the court, or what standard the court applies in deciding one; this clause does not supply any of those. The section's reference to "the tax consequences to each party" is a reservation of jurisdiction, not a statement of any tax rule; federal and California income tax treatment of a residence sale is governed by tax statutes outside the Family Code that this clause neither quotes nor summarizes. Section 3809's reservation is distinct from the modification and termination provisions of sections 3807 and 3808, which are addressed in separate clauses of this document.

MODIFICATION OR TERMINATION OF THE ORDER — FAMILY CODE SECTION 3807
Family Code section 3807 provides that, except as otherwise agreed to by the parties in writing, a deferred sale of home order may be modified or terminated at any time at the discretion of the court. Two features appear on the face of the section. First, the court's power to modify or terminate is stated without a time limit and is committed to the court's discretion. Second, the section opens with an express carve-out for a written agreement of the parties, so the default rule it states is one the parties may address by written agreement.

Section 3807 does not state what showing supports a modification or termination, what procedure applies, or what the court must find; the rebuttable presumption created by section 3808 on remarriage or a change in circumstances is a separate provision addressed in this document's companion clause, and this clause does not restate it. The section's opening carve-out refers to what "the parties" have "otherwise agreed to ... in writing" but does not state what such a writing must contain, when it must be made, or whether and how it must be approved or incorporated by the court; this clause does not address those points, nor does it address the separate body of California law on the enforceability of marital agreements, which is covered by other statutes and by separate information sheets in this corpus.

THE REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION ON REMARRIAGE OR A CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES — FAMILY CODE SECTION 3808 AND IN RE MARRIAGE OF BRAUD
Family Code section 3808 provides that, except as otherwise agreed to by the parties in writing, if the party awarded the deferred sale of home order remarries, or if there is otherwise a change in circumstances affecting the determinations made under section 3801 or 3802 or affecting the economic status of the parties or the children on which the award is based, a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof is created that further deferral of the sale is no longer an equitable method of minimizing the adverse impact of the dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties on the children. In In re Marriage of Braud (1996) 45 Cal.App.4th 797, the Court of Appeal addressed a nonresident parent's contention that the resident parent's nonmarital cohabitation was itself a "remarriage" or change in circumstances under section 3808. Reviewing the history of the statute and its predecessors, the court stated that in the original "family home award" legislation and in every amendment and recodification since 1984 the Legislature had decided that cohabitation, by itself, was not sufficient to trigger a statutory presumption against further deferral.

THE CHAPTER'S APPLICABILITY RULE AND THE ABSENCE OF A SECTION 3805 — FAMILY CODE SECTION 3810
Family Code section 3810 provides that the deferred sale of home order chapter is applicable regardless of whether the deferred sale of home order is made before or after January 1, 1989 — a date that corresponds to the operative date of the chapter's immediate predecessor in the Civil Code. A second, purely structural point is observable in the published code text: the chapter is captioned "Deferred Sale of Home Order [3800 - 3810]" and its published text runs through sections 3800, 3801, 3802, 3803, 3804, 3806, 3807, 3808, 3809, and 3810; no section 3805 appears in the chapter's current published text.

THE DOCTRINE'S JUDICIAL ORIGIN — IN RE MARRIAGE OF DUKE (1980)
The practice that the Legislature later codified in Family Code sections 3800 through 3810 is commonly traced to In re Marriage of Duke (1980) 101 Cal.App.3d 152, decided years before the statutory chapter existed, and an order deferring the sale of a family home is still often called a "Duke order." In Duke, the Court of Appeal reversed the portion of an interlocutory dissolution judgment that ordered immediate sale of the family residence, holding that the trial court had failed to exercise proper discretion when it rejected the custodial parent's request to defer the sale without balancing the emotional, economic, and social impacts of an immediate sale on the family unit against the foreseeable detriment to the noncustodial spouse. The court stated that the subjective, noneconomic impact on the family unit of being deprived of a home environment to which the children had become accustomed was significant enough to allow a court to enter such a conditional order, so long as undue hardship was not imposed on the noncustodial parent, and it described the circumstances in which the unique relationship of the home to the family calls for an analysis of all relevant factors in light of the length of the delay requested.

JUDICIAL CONSTRUCTION OF THE CHAPTER'S SCOPE AND THE DISCRETIONARY NATURE OF THE ORDER — IN RE MARRIAGE OF BRAUD (1996)
In In re Marriage of Braud (1996) 45 Cal.App.4th 797, the Court of Appeal construed the deferred sale of home order chapter in a case where the home was a "mixed asset" in which the nonresident spouse held a separate property interest. Three points from that opinion describe the chapter's reach. First, the court observed that the statutory scheme nowhere defines the term "family home." Second, reading the chapter together with Family Code section 4008, which provides that community, quasi-community, and separate property may be subjected to the support of children in the proportions the court determines are just, the court stated that those provisions can be viewed as authorizing deferred sale of home orders that impinge upon the separate property interests of out-spouses who are also child-support obligors. Third, on the discretionary character of the order, the court stated that a deferred sale of home order is never mandatory and that, so long as the threshold statutory requirement of economic feasibility is met, the trial court has broad discretion to grant or deny a request for such an order.

expectedJSON.body: This Deferred Sale of Home Order Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, whose proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties is pending, has concluded by judgment, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes what California law says about a "deferred sale of home order" — the order, sometimes called a "Duke order" after the decision that first approved the practice, by which a California family court temporarily delays the sale of the family home and awards its temporary exclusive use and possession to a custodial parent. It states, in general terms, the statutory definitions in Family Code section 3800, the threshold economic-feasibility determination required by section 3801, the discretionary factors listed in section 3802, what the order must and may contain under sections 3803, 3804, and 3806, the reservation of jurisdiction required by section 3809, the modification and termination provisions of sections 3807 and 3808, the chapter's applicability rule in section 3810, and how two published California decisions have described the doctrine's judicial origin and its statutory scope. This information sheet does not determine, calculate, or assert that a deferred sale of home order would or would not be economically feasible in the circumstances of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, that any such order is or is not necessary to minimize the adverse impact of the proceeding on any child, how any listed factor weighs on these facts, or whether any change in circumstances has occurred; those are matters for the court to decide on the specific evidence before it, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to address by their own written agreement.

Family Code section 3800 supplies the three defined terms used throughout the chapter on deferred sale of home orders (Family Code sections 3800 through 3810). Subdivision (a) defines "custodial parent" as a party awarded physical custody of a child. Subdivision (b) defines a "deferred sale of home order" as an order that temporarily delays the sale of the family home and awards its temporary exclusive use and possession to a custodial parent of a minor child, or of a child for whom support is authorized under Family Code sections 3900 and 3901 (support of a minor child and of an unmarried full-time high school student under 19) or under section 3910 (support of an adult child incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means), whether or not the custodial parent has sole or joint custody, in order to minimize the adverse impact of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties on the welfare of the child. Subdivision (c) defines "resident parent" as a party who has requested, or who has already been awarded, a deferred sale of home order. By the terms of subdivision (b), the order is an order about the timing of a sale and about temporary use and possession; the definition does not describe it as an award of ownership of the home to either party.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 3801 sets a threshold the court addresses before it reaches the discretionary question. Subdivision (a) provides that if one of the parties has requested a deferred sale of home order, the court shall first determine whether it is economically feasible to maintain the payments on any note secured by a deed of trust, the property taxes, and the insurance for the home during the period the sale is deferred, and to maintain the condition of the home comparable to its condition at the time of trial. Subdivision (b) directs the court, in making that determination, to consider all of three listed items: the resident parent's income; the availability of spousal support, child support, or both; and any other sources of funds available to make those payments. Subdivision (c) states the Legislature's declared intent in requiring the determination — to avoid the likelihood of possible defaults on note payments and resulting foreclosures, to avoid inadequate insurance coverage, to prevent deterioration of the condition of the family home, and to prevent any other circumstance that would jeopardize both parents' equity in the home.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 3802 governs the decision itself. Subdivision (a) provides that if the court has determined under section 3801 that it is economically feasible to consider ordering a deferred sale of the family home, the court may grant a deferred sale of home order to a custodial parent if the court determines that the order is necessary in order to minimize the adverse impact of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties on the child. The verb is permissive — the court "may" grant the order — and the necessity finding is a precondition to granting it. Subdivision (b) provides that in exercising its discretion to grant or deny the order the court shall consider all of ten listed factors: the length of time the child has resided in the home; the child's placement or grade in school; the accessibility and convenience of the home to the child's school and other services or facilities used by and available to the child, including child care; whether the home has been adapted or modified to accommodate any physical disabilities of a child or a resident parent in a manner that a change in residence may adversely affect the resident parent's ability to meet the child's needs; the emotional detriment to the child associated with a change in residence; the extent to which the location of the home permits the resident parent to continue employment; the financial ability of each parent to obtain suitable housing; the tax consequences to the parents; the economic detriment to the nonresident parent in the event of a deferred sale of home order; and any other factors the court deems just and equitable.

expectedJSON.body: Three sections of the chapter address the content and mechanics of the order. Family Code section 3803 provides that a deferred sale of home order shall state the duration of the order and may include the legal description and the assessor's parcel number of the real property subject to the order — the duration is mandatory content, the property identifiers are optional content. Family Code section 3804 provides that a deferred sale of home order may be recorded in the office of the county recorder of the county in which the real property is located; recording is permissive under the statute's own terms, not required. Family Code section 3806 provides that the court may make an order specifying the parties' respective responsibilities for the payment of the costs of routine maintenance and of capital improvements.

Reviewing the history of the statute and its predecessors, the court stated that in the original "family home award" legislation and in every amendment and recodification since 1984 the Legislature had decided that cohabitation, by itself, was not sufficient to trigger a statutory presumption against further deferral.

expectedJSON.body: The practice that the Legislature later codified in Family Code sections 3800 through 3810 is commonly traced to In re Marriage of Duke (1980) 101 Cal.App.3d 152, decided years before the statutory chapter existed, and an order deferring the sale of a family home is still often called a "Duke order." In Duke, the Court of Appeal reversed the portion of an interlocutory dissolution judgment that ordered immediate sale of the family residence, holding that the trial court had failed to exercise proper discretion when it rejected the custodial parent's request to defer the sale without balancing the emotional, economic, and social impacts of an immediate sale on the family unit against the foreseeable detriment to the noncustodial spouse. The court stated that the subjective, noneconomic impact on the family unit of being deprived of a home environment to which the children had become accustomed was significant enough to allow a court to enter such a conditional order, so long as undue hardship was not imposed on the noncustodial parent, and it described the circumstances in which the unique relationship of the home to the family calls for an analysis of all relevant factors in light of the length of the delay requested.

Three points from that opinion describe the chapter's reach. First, the court observed that the statutory scheme nowhere defines the term "family home." Second, reading the chapter together with Family Code section 4008, which provides that community, quasi-community, and separate property may be subjected to the support of children in the proportions the court determines are just, the court stated that those provisions can be viewed as authorizing deferred sale of home orders that impinge upon the separate property interests of out-spouses who are also child-support obligors. Third, on the discretionary character of the order, the court stated that a deferred sale of home order is never mandatory and that, so long as the threshold statutory requirement of economic feasibility is met, the trial court has broad discretion to grant or deny a request for such an order.

Family Code section 4008 is quoted inside the Braud opinion and is not separately fetched or quoted here. Whether any particular residence is a "family home," whether any party is a child-support obligor, and how a court would exercise its discretion on given facts are questions for the court, and this clause does not address them.
